w:r.w:t: Final Project · 5th Year Architecture · Ariel University, 2022
Student Dormitories as an Architectural Laboratory for Communal Living
Architecture as a dynamic, data-informed laboratory — where spatial design is continuously measured, iterated, and validated against lived human outcomes.
NKDT Project Cover Render / Site Aerial — Ariel New Dorms Complex
Ariel University, Ariel, Israel — proposed community dormitory complex

Two conditions define the architectural opportunity of the moment. First, the exponential growth of available data has made it possible to move beyond intuition: nearly every person carries a device capable of generating spatial telemetry, and data-informed design allows architects to find patterns in complex systems and compare alternatives against real conditions. Second — and equally urgent — loneliness is an epidemic. It is a subjective state distinct from social isolation: even people embedded in large networks can feel its absence of depth. Architecture has a concrete role to play in reversing this, through spaces that actively foster layered belonging and spontaneous encounter.
Information-driven design — data feedback loop diagram
Loneliness epidemic — community bond erosion diagram
Data-feedback cycle enabling iterative spatial improvement (left) · Erosion of community bonds since the Renaissance (right)

The project synthesises both imperatives into one programme: an architectural laboratory for communal living, built on the platform of student dormitories. The three pillars are inseparable — the dormitory provides the controlled institutional context; the communal design addresses loneliness through layered shared space; the laboratory framing makes every design decision a testable, measurable hypothesis.
Dynamic system built for continuous spatial experimentation — designed to change and extract insights during active operation.
Design against loneliness: layered shared spaces that invite spontaneous contact, graduated privacy, and resident ownership of collective ground.
The platform: institutional ownership + cross-sectional transient population + medium-term tenancy = ideal conditions for iterative spatial research.

Ariel University presents a rare natural experiment: two radically opposed dormitory compounds on the same campus, serving the same population — a corridor / mid-rise cluster (inside/outside the fence, ~760 beds, institutional character) against a scattered caravan plex (organically distributed across topography, ~1,240 beds, village atmosphere). The contrast is stark enough to test foundational assumptions about how spatial configuration shapes community, while institutional ownership and population cross-section make the data tractable.

The current campus is structurally fragmented: dorms split between inside and outside the university fence create two communities with different characters; the campus itself is bisected by a road; and dormitories already occupy ~50% of the built footprint — with rapid growth demanding densification. Yet the buffer position between university and city carries genuine connective potential, currently squandered.
Ariel University aerial map — existing dorm compounds highlighted
Existing campus: corridor compound (outside fence, left) vs scattered caravan compound (inside campus, right)
New Ariel masterplan — topographic contours, circulation, building footprints, neighbourhood divisions
New Ariel: dorms repositioned as community buffer between city and campus — topographically embedded across 28 plots in 7 neighbourhoods

Four moves structure the proposal: the dorm buffer becomes a connector enabling daily student-resident interaction; a peripheral ring road and central plaza reunite the split campus; 28 plots group into 7 neighbourhoods with shared identity, colour, and community programme; and three distinct building typologies distribute across the site to enable spatial comparison.
Flexible Repetition — The Modular Design System

The design logic rests on a single repeated apartment module whose placement — not its internal configuration — generates spatial variety. Community emerges from the interstitial spaces created between modules: the corridor as shared living room, the sectional void as cross-floor encounter zone, the facade gap as neighbourhood balcony.
Private room — section A-A: workspace + storage + sleeping mezzanine
Apartment unit — floor plan: 2–4 rooms around shared living / kitchen
Room provides minimum private programme without replacing shared space · Apartment bridges room and collective floor with a designed privacy gradient
Apartment unit exploded axonometric — privacy hierarchy from entry (open) to bedroom (private)
Ceiling height and sightlines calibrate the transition from fully open (kitchen/living) to fully private (bedroom)
The same module deploys in three configurations, each testing a different social hypothesis across 28 plots:
6 floors · corridor-based · ground-floor commercial · rooftop community · main boulevard
4 floors · cluster-based · follows topography · internal promenade · topographic community spaces
3 floors · no fixed boundary · scattered plex · community in spatial voids · most communal character
Type A — Urban corridor typology, building section & facade
Type B — Mixed cluster typology, floor plan & section
Type C — Rural scattered typology, site plan & section
Three typologies, one module — spatial variation emerges from configuration, not from different unit designs

The corridor is not a circulation spine — it is a shared living room. The section is not a stack of floors — it is a social landscape. The facade is not a boundary — it is a membrane of controlled exposure.

Each floor uses a structural grid that can hold more apartments than are placed. The resulting spatial voids — at varying scales — create communal niches from large shared lounges to intimate alcoves. Shared wall configurations let residents control the degree of openness between their apartment and the floor corridor. Sectional offsets between floors, deliberate stairwell incursion into residential levels, and staggered facade balconies extend the social field vertically.
Axonometric — 'breathing building': stairwell incursion, offset floors, staggered balconies
The building section as a social instrument: vertical movement as communal encounter
Grounded in Evidence — The Seminar Research

This design is not speculative. Its typological strategy is directly grounded in a prior empirical study — Student Dorms Archetype as a Driving Factor in the Formation of a Sense of Community (Ariel University, 2022) — which used SCI-2 and URES psychometric instruments alongside passive GPS telemetry to compare the two existing Ariel compounds. The caravan scattered-plex scored 3.9/5 on spatial quality against the mid-rise cluster's 2.9/5, with corresponding quantitative differences in Sense of Community. Those findings — which spatial features drive belonging and which suppress it — shaped the void strategy, the privacy gradient, the typology mix, and the community-space hierarchy across all three building types. The measurement infrastructure (NKDT Points app, privacy-by-design GPS pipeline) developed for that study becomes the lab's ongoing instrument.
Seminar: SCI-2 bar chart — caravan vs mid-rise compound scores
Seminar: Qualitative spatial scores — 7 parameters, both compounds
Seminar findings feeding directly into the NKDT design hypothesis — scattered-plex spatial DNA embedded in all three typologies

As the complex operates, data accumulates across semesters — SCI-2, URES, GPA delta, GPS telemetry — and informs incremental modifications to void placement, shared-wall positions, and community programme. The building evolves toward greater community efficacy through empirical iteration rather than speculative one-off design.
Feedback loop diagram: spatial design → data collection → statistical analysis → incremental update → repeat
Architecture-as-laboratory: each spatial iteration is simultaneously intervention and measurement

The truest architectural ambition of NKDT is not the building itself — it is the methodology: a proof of concept that spatial quality can be measured, iterated, and progressively refined, replacing intuition with evidence at every scale from the private room to the city edge.
